transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. AI. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. AI. Well, I guess... I mean, I am here because things have been getting a little strange lately. I work as a bookkeeping clerk, you know, doing accounting stuff, mostly data entry and reconciling accounts, which usually I am completely fine at. But recently I have been doing these things at work and at school that just... they do not really make any sense at all. 

Like, the other day, instead of just entering the expenses into the spreadsheet like I am supposed to, I took all the physical receipts. There were probably like fifty or sixty of them from the last month, and I just started lining them up across the floor. End to end, all the way across the carpet. I do not even really know why, I just did it. And then, when I sit at my desk, I have this heavy-duty calculator for my audits, and I have been tapping the keys, but I keep doing it in sets of nine. Just tapping nine times. Over and over. If I lose count, I have to start the set of nine completely over, and it takes up so much of my shift, but I just sit there tapping it. 

But the weirdest part is when I go to make copies. I will go into the copy room, and I just end up standing right by the copier with my hands held up in the air. Just holding them up by my head. And I will stand there like that for who knows how long until someone walks in and asks if I am okay. My supervisor actually walked in on Tuesday and asked what in the world I was doing, and only then did I put my hands down and snap out of it. So, I guess that is why I came in, because I just cannot explain why I am acting like this and it is taking up so much of my day.
When you do these things, do you have upsetting thoughts or fears that you feel you have to neutralize?

Well, no, it's not really like that at all. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, you know, "If I don't tap this calculator exactly nine times, the office is going to burn down" or something. I know some people get those kinds of fears, but for me, there isn't any worry or bad thought I'm trying to fix or neutralize. It's honestly just... my mind is almost completely disconnected from any kind of fear. 

Like when I was doing that thing with the receipts on the floor. I wasn't scared of anything happening. I just looked at the pile of paper, and the next thing I know, I'm down on my hands and knees on that awful, scratchy gray office carpet—the kind that always gives you a static shock whenever you touch the metal filing cabinets—and I'm just lining them up. Edge to edge. There were no thoughts about preventing a disaster or anything. 

And the same goes for standing by the copier. It's so strange, because I'm definitely not afraid of the machine, and I'm not trying to push away some terrible thought. My arms just sort of go up by my head. And I just stay there. It's almost like someone just hit the pause button on me, but there's absolutely no scary thought or anxiety behind it. I just exist in that position until someone walks in and breaks the spell. So, no, I don't have any upsetting thoughts driving it, which honestly almost makes it more confusing for me, because if I'm not trying to fix a bad thought, then why am I even doing it, right?
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people do not?

Well, yeah, actually... I mean, it's not all the time, but it happens enough that I've definitely noticed it, and it's really starting to bother me. Sometimes, especially when I'm just sitting alone at my desk—you know, when the office is quiet and everyone else is on their lunch break, or maybe when I'm just walking home from my evening classes and the streets are pretty empty—I hear this voice. 

It's a man's voice. And it's not like a whisper or a thought in my head, it sounds exactly like someone is standing right behind me or just over my shoulder. He says these really specific things, too. Like, the other day I was looking at a spreadsheet, and I heard him say, as clear as day, "check line seven." And I spun around in my chair so fast I almost knocked over my coffee mug, because I was absolutely certain my supervisor or one of the senior accountants had walked up behind me. But there was literally no one there. The whole cubicle aisle was empty. 

And then another time, I was just walking down the sidewalk, minding my own business, carrying my backpack—which is always so heavy because of my accounting textbooks—and I heard that same man's voice say, "you missed the sign." Again, so loud and clear. I stopped right in my tracks and looked all around, up and down the street, checking behind cars and looking into store windows to see who was talking to me. But there was just nobody around who could have said it. It's so strange, because the voice is so real, so solid, but there's never a physical person attached to it. I just don't understand where it's coming from, but it definitely makes me jump every single time it happens.
Have you had any strong fixed beliefs that other people say are not true?

Well, yes... I mean, people tell me they aren't true, but to me, it feels so real, you know? It's honestly been a huge issue at work. I know it sounds completely strange, and I've tried to explain it to my supervisor, but he just looks at me like I'm crazy. 

See, I work with numbers all day. Spreadsheets, invoices, ledgers, all of it. And lately, I've just become completely convinced that certain invoice totals, specific account numbers, and even the due dates on these accounts... they're not just random business numbers. They're messages. About me. 

Like, for example, last Thursday, I was reconciling the accounts for one of our biggest vendors—a paper supply company we've used for years—and I noticed the invoice total was exactly $1,444. And then the account number ended in 44. And the due date was April 4th. And I just... I knew. I knew right then and there that it was a message specifically directed at me. It felt like someone, or something, was trying to tell me something, or maybe testing me to see if I could figure it out. 

My supervisor, Mr. Henderson—he's this older guy, very practical, always wears these terrible patterned ties—he actually sat down with me. He brought up the vendor's history on his monitor and showed me, line by line, that these were completely normal entries. He showed me the purchase orders, the shipping receipts, everything. He was trying to prove to me that it was just a regular transaction. And logically, I hear what he's saying, I really do. But even after he showed me all that proof, I couldn't shake the feeling. I still feel, deep down in my gut, like they are tracking me. Like they're monitoring whether I understand the pattern they're laying out for me in the numbers. 

And it's not just that one time, either. I find myself scanning every single document that comes across my desk, looking for these patterns, trying to decode what they mean for me. It takes up so much time, and I know Mr. Henderson is getting frustrated because my productivity has tanked, but I just can't ignore it when it feels so incredibly real. It's like I'm the only one who can see the truth hidden in the data, even when everyone else insists it's just regular accounting.
Have other people told you that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another in a way that is hard to understand?

Yeah, actually, that has been happening a lot lately. Mr. Henderson, my supervisor, the one I mentioned earlier with the terrible ties, he actually pulled me aside about this just the other day. I was trying to explain to him why this one particular ledger was off by a few hundred dollars. It was supposed to be a simple reconciliation issue, but in my head, there was this whole web of connections that he needed to understand to really get why the numbers were behaving that way.

So, I started out talking about the ledger, right? But then I realized the date on the discrepancy was the exact same date as my tuition deadline for my evening classes. So I started explaining that to him, because the timing felt incredibly relevant to the whole situation. And from the tuition deadline, my brain just naturally went to tax rules, because of the education credits and how they overlap with the quarterly filings we were working on. 

But then, while I was explaining the tax rules, I remembered this specific invoice we had processed for a client who bought all this expensive studio lighting equipment. And I started talking about how the depreciation on the studio lighting tied into those same tax rules, and how the totals on the lighting invoice perfectly matched the number patterns I have been seeing everywhere. The patterns I told you about earlier that are tracking me. 

So I am standing there, trying to lay all this out for him, explaining how the ledger discrepancy, the tuition deadlines, the tax rules, the studio lighting, and the number patterns are all completely connected... and he just put his hands up. He stopped me and said he had absolutely no idea what I was talking about. He told me I was jumping from one completely unrelated idea to another and that he could not follow how I got from a basic ledger error to studio lighting and my tuition. 

And it is so frustrating, you know? Because to me, it makes perfect sense. It is a straight line in my head. Every piece of information leads directly to the next. But when I try to explain it out loud, I guess all the connections get tangled up for other people. They just stare at me. It is not just him, either, a couple of the other clerks have mentioned that my explanations are just too hard to track lately because I jump around too much.
Have you been having periods where you stay completely still or mute, as if you cannot move or speak?

Well, not exactly like I am paralyzed or anything, but... actually, yes, in a way, I do freeze up. That is actually a huge part of why I finally came in to see you in the first place, because I have started doing things at work and at school that just completely do not make any sense, even to me when I look back on them. 

Like the staying still thing you just mentioned. The other day I was in the copy room at the office—it is this cramped little room right next to the break area that always smells intensely like toner and burnt coffee—and I had gone in there to run off some copies of the quarterly expense reports. But instead of making the copies, I just stopped. I lifted my hands up in the air, almost like I was surrendering to someone, and I just stood by the copier completely still. I did not move a single muscle, and I did not say a word. I have no idea how long I was standing there like a statue, just staring blankly ahead with my hands up, until Brenda from HR came in to grab her printouts and she had to ask me if I was okay. It was only when she spoke to me that I finally snapped out of it and put my arms down. 

And it is not just freezing up like that, either. I have been doing other really strange things that are taking up so much of my time. Like, I will take a massive stack of travel receipts from the sales team—they always hand them to me completely crumpled and out of order—and instead of entering them into the ledger software, I will get down on my hands and knees and start lining the receipts all the way across the floor of my cubicle. I just lay them out end-to-end in these long, straight lines across the carpet. 

Or, when I am supposed to be doing data entry, I will just stop typing and start tapping on my ten-key calculator. Not even pushing the buttons to do math, just tapping the plastic casing with my fingernail, and I have to do it in exact sets of nine. Tap, tap, tap... exactly nine times, over and over again. I do it at my desk, I do it during my evening lectures at school with my phone calculator... I just get stuck doing these bizarre things, like the tapping or the lining things up or standing frozen by the copier, and I don't know why I am doing them, but I just can't seem to stop myself.
Have people noticed that your emotions or facial expression seem unusually flat or reduced lately?

Yeah, actually, my roommate and a couple of my friends from school have definitely noticed that. They say I just look... blank all the time now. And it is really strange because I still care about people, I really do. It is not like I am mad at anyone or that I have suddenly stopped caring about my friends. But most days, I just... I don't know, I just don't have it in me to react to anything. 

Like, my phone will buzz, and I will see a text from my buddy Dave, or from the group chat I have with the guys from my evening classes, and I will read it, but I just let the texts sit there completely unanswered. Sometimes for days at a time. The energy it takes to just type back a simple "yeah" or "cool" just feels completely out of reach. And it is the exact same with seeing them in person. Usually, after my Tuesday and Thursday lectures, a bunch of us would go grab food at this diner near campus, just to decompress and hang out before going home. But lately, the second class ends, I just pack up my bag and walk straight to my car. I completely skip hanging out after class now. They will call out to me to see if I'm coming, and I just kind of give a half-wave and leave. 

And the thing that really bothers them, I think, is that even when I am around them, I just don't react to anything anymore. They will be talking about things that I used to absolutely love. We used to go to all these local underground music shows downtown, these really loud, high-energy gigs, or we would get together on weekends and work on these big, messy collaborative art projects. I used to be the one getting everyone hyped up about that stuff. But now, they will be talking about a new band playing this weekend or some new art thing they want to do, and I just feel completely flat inside. I just sit there staring at them. I know I should be smiling or getting excited, but my face just doesn't do anything. I can tell it makes them uncomfortable because I am just giving them this completely reduced, empty expression while they are talking about stuff we used to be so passionate about.
When you hold those frozen positions, does someone else ever try to move your arms or legs, and do they stay in that same position afterward?

Well, no, not really. No one has actually tried to physically grab my arms or move my legs when I get stuck like that. 

Like, if we go back to that time in the copy room with Brenda from HR that I was just telling you about... when she walked in and I was just standing there with my hands up in the air by the toner machine. She was just standing there by the door holding this huge stack of manila folders—the thick ones with the reinforced tabs that we use for the end-of-year audits, because she's always running those reports on Thursdays—and she just looked completely confused. But she didn't step closer to pull my arms down or try to adjust my posture or anything like that. She just kind of hovered near the doorframe and used her voice. 

I think people are honestly just too polite, or maybe a little too weirded out, to actually come up and physically manipulate my limbs. Like, if you see a guy standing like a statue in the middle of the office, your first instinct isn't usually to walk over and start bending his elbows for him, you know? You just ask him what he's doing. And the second someone actually talks to me, like when Brenda finally said my name, or like the other night when my roommate accidentally bumped into my desk chair while I was stuck staring at the wall in our apartment, the spell just sort of breaks. I just put my arms down on my own. 

So, no, nobody has ever molded me into a pose and left me there like a store mannequin or anything. I don't think they would even get the chance to try, because just the shock of them speaking to me or entering my personal space is usually enough to snap me out of whatever weird holding pattern my brain is stuck in. Though, I do sit and wonder sometimes what would happen if they didn't say anything and just walked up and tried to push my arm down. Like, would my arm feel heavy? Would I resist them? Would I just let them move me? I really couldn't tell you, because it just hasn't happened. They always just use their words, and then I realize how ridiculous I must look standing there, and I just drop my hands and try to pretend I was just stretching or something.
If someone gently moved one of your arms or legs into a position, would it stay there as if it were waxy or molded?

Like I was trying to explain a second ago, I really couldn't tell you if my arm would stay there like wax or clay, because nobody has ever actually tried to pose me. It’s... well, honestly, it's not really about someone else moving my body. The real issue—the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place—is that I have started doing all these things at work and at school that just do not make any sense at all. 

I mean, like I mentioned with the copier, just standing there with my hands held up in the air for absolutely no reason until someone finally asks if I am okay. That right there makes no sense. But it’s not just that. It’s the other stuff I was telling you about, too, where I just get totally derailed from what I'm supposed to be doing. Like taking those crumpled travel receipts from the sales guys and, instead of actually doing my auditing work and typing the numbers into the system, I'm getting down on my hands and knees on the floor. I just start lining them up, end-to-end, all the way across the cubicle carpet, making these long trails of paper. 

Or I'll be sitting in my evening classes, or at my desk at the office, and I just start tapping the side of my calculator. Not even doing math, just tapping the plastic casing in exact sets of nine, over and over again. I just don't understand why I am doing any of this. The tapping in nines, the lining the receipts up across the floor, the standing by the toner machine with my hands up... none of it makes sense to me, but it’s taking over my days, and I just... I don't know why my brain is making me do these things.
When you freeze up, are you completely unresponsive to people trying to get your attention?

No, no, I wouldn't say I am completely unresponsive. It is actually... well, it is kind of the opposite, really. Like I was trying to say a minute ago, if someone says my name or even just makes a loud enough noise, it breaks the whole spell completely. 

Take my roommate, for instance. The other night I was sitting at my desk—it is this really cheap particle-board desk I got off Craigslist when we first moved into our apartment, the kind where the fake wood veneer is already peeling off the corners because it is so old—and I was just frozen there. I was just staring blankly at the drywall right above where I keep my work calendar. I think I had been sitting there for maybe twenty minutes, just totally locked up, not moving a single muscle. And my roommate was out in the kitchen making dinner, boiling pasta or something, and he came into my room to ask if I wanted some. 

He didn't even yell, he just asked me if I was hungry and accidentally nudged the back of my desk chair with his knee while he was standing there. And the very second he spoke and the chair moved, it was like... I don't know, like a switch flipped. I immediately blinked and turned my head and answered him. I told him I was fine and didn't need any food. So I definitely hear people. It is not like I am deaf or totally checked out of reality or locked inside my own head. My ears still work perfectly fine, and my brain processes that someone is talking to me. 

If Brenda at the office says my name, or my roommate asks me a question, or honestly even if a delivery truck honks really loud outside my bedroom window, I snap right back to normal and respond to them. So no, definitely not completely unresponsive. I just need that little external push to get my gears turning again, I guess. And then, of course, I always feel incredibly awkward right after, because I have to act like I wasn't just sitting there like a literal statue. I usually try to play it off, like I pretend I was just deep in thought about an audit report for work or trying to remember a specific tax formula for my evening classes, but I know they probably think it is super weird anyway. But yeah, I always respond when they actually try to get my attention.
When you stand with your hands up by the copier, do you feel as if an outside force is making your body do that?

No, no, nothing like that. I can see why you might ask that, though, like maybe I feel like a puppet on strings or something. But honestly, no. It isn't like some invisible hand is pulling my arms up, or like there's some kind of... I don't know, ghost or magnetic force or mind-control thing happening. It is definitely just me. My own muscles, my own bones. 

When I am standing there by that copier—the big heavy-duty one on the third floor that always smells faintly like burnt plastic when you run more than fifty pages through it at once—it is entirely my own body doing the action. It's just that I don't understand *why* my body is doing it. That's the part that drives me crazy. Like, I know it is my brain sending the signal to lift my hands up, but I just don't know why it's sending that signal in the first place. 

I've actually thought about this a lot. Like, I will be sitting on the bus on my way home from the office—I take the 42 line down past the old shopping center because my car has been making this awful grinding noise in the steering column and I just haven't had the time or the money to take it into a mechanic yet—and I will just be staring out the window, replaying the whole situation with Brenda in my head. And I'll ask myself, 'Did I feel forced? Did someone else make me do that?' And the answer is always no. 

There is no outside pressure, no heavy feeling of someone else guiding my limbs. It is more like... like a glitch in my own programming, if that makes sense. Like my body just decides to hit pause on its own accord and strike this bizarre pose, and my conscious mind is just sort of trapped watching it happen, thinking, 'What in the world are we doing right now?' But it's always me. Just my own confusing, frustrating brain acting up, not any kind of outside force.
When you freeze up like that, are you unable to move at all?

I honestly couldn't tell you if I'm literally unable to move, because... well, because in those moments, the very concept of moving just completely evaporates from my mind. It’s not like I'm fighting against my own body, you know? 

It's not like that sleep paralysis thing. I had a buddy in high school, Jason, who used to get sleep paralysis all the time, and he said it was absolutely terrifying because he would wake up in the middle of the night and try so, so hard to thrash around or yell for his mom, and his body just wouldn't let him do it. He was actively trying to move and couldn't. 

For me, it is nothing like that at all. There is no struggle. When I'm standing by that heavy-duty copier on the third floor, or when I'm staring at the drywall above my peeling particle-board desk, I'm not fighting to put my arms down or turn my head. I'm just... there. The thought of lowering my hands or walking back to my cubicle just doesn't even cross my mind until Brenda says my name or my roommate bumps my chair. 

So I guess I don't really know if I am physically unable to move, because I have never actually tried to break out of it myself while it's happening. It's like my brain just temporarily deletes the instructions for movement, or hits pause on the whole system. My muscles aren't cramped up, I don't feel paralyzed or heavy, but the actual internal command to move just isn't there. So I really can't say for sure if I'm trapped in that position or not, because it never even occurs to me to test the boundaries of it until someone finally snaps me out of it.
When you stand frozen like that, do you also become completely mute?

Well, I guess I am quiet during it, yeah, but I wouldn't say I'm permanently mute or anything because, like I was saying, the second someone actually speaks to me, I answer them right away. But until they do... yeah, I'm not making a peep. Honestly, though, the not speaking part isn't even the main reason I finally decided to come in and see you. I came in because I have started doing all these things at work and school that just do not make any sense whatsoever, and it's really starting to freak me out. 

Like, it's not just the freezing up. The other day at work—I'm a bookkeeping and auditing clerk, so I deal with a ton of paperwork and expense reports—I was supposed to be reconciling these travel expenses, and instead of typing them into the system, I just started lining all the receipts across the floor. Just laying them out, end to end, perfectly straight all the way across the ugly gray carpet in my cubicle. I wasn't even reading the amounts on them, just lining them up. 

And I'll do this weird thing with my calculator, too. I have this really loud, clacky 10-key calculator on my desk for audits, and I will just sit there tapping the keys in sets of nine. Exactly nine taps, over and over again, for no logical reason at all. It makes absolutely no sense. 

And then, of course, there's the thing we were just talking about, standing by the copier with my hands held up in the air, just completely silent and frozen, until someone finally walks by and asks if I am okay. Once they ask if I'm alright, I can talk perfectly fine again and I put my hands down. So I'm not mute, I just... I don't say anything while I'm stuck doing these bizarre, pointless things until someone breaks the spell. I just don't get why I'm doing any of it, but it's happening at the office, it's happening during my evening classes, and I just really need to figure out what's wrong with my brain.
Have you ever had periods of becoming unusually energetic, agitated, or driven to move around in a way that seems out of control?

Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It's actually kind of a total 180 from the freezing up thing we were just talking about. It's like... well, it's like a switch flips, and suddenly I have all this buzzing inside my chest and my arms. When that energy comes on, I absolutely cannot sit through a normal bookkeeping shift. I mean, my job is literally just sitting in a chair for eight hours staring at spreadsheets and typing numbers into the system, but when I get like that, sitting still feels physically impossible. It almost hurts to stay seated.

I end up getting up and pacing back and forth in my cubicle—which isn't very big, so it's really just three steps one way, three steps back, over and over again, wearing a path in that same ugly gray carpet I mentioned earlier. And if I try to force myself to sit down and actually do my work, my hands just feel like they need to keep moving. Like they have a motor attached to them. I'll just start opening extra tabs on my computer for no reason. Like, dozens of them. I'll have the company portal open, and then I'll open a tab for a web calculator, and then a blank Google sheet, and then a search for office supplies, just click-click-clicking because my fingers can't stop moving. 

And then I'll look at the physical files on my desk and suddenly decide the entire system is wrong, so I'll start reorganizing files. I'll take all these manila folders—the ones with the little clear plastic tabs that always cut your cuticles if you grab them the wrong way—and I'll pull out all the expense reports and start sorting them by date instead of by vendor name, which isn't even how we're supposed to do it. Brenda actually got really annoyed with me about it last month because she couldn't find the Miller account. But in the moment, I just have so much frantic, nervous energy that I have to be doing *something*, anything, just moving and clicking and sorting at a million miles an hour. It's like I'm driven by this invisible engine and I just can't figure out how to hit the brakes.
During those times when you feel unusually energetic and driven to move, do you also feel abnormally euphoric or overly confident?

Yeah, euphoric is... I mean, confident doesn't even really begin to cover it. It's more like... well, some weeks I just feel unusually sharp, you know? Like my brain is finally operating at a hundred percent capacity and I am just almost completely unstoppable. I'll get home from my evening classes and I won't even be tired. I'll just sit at my particle-board desk in my room and feel like I can map out my entire future in one single night. 

I'll start making these massive, incredibly detailed master plans. Because I'm a clerk, right? So I know how to organize data. I'll start charting out exactly how I'm going to finish my degree early, pass the CPA exam on the first try, start my own auditing firm, and make my first million by the time I'm twenty-five. I'll literally make color-coded spreadsheets for my life goals at three in the morning, and I feel so brilliant while I'm doing it. I feel like I'm the only person on earth who actually understands how the world works, and it's this huge rush. 

But the thing is, it's not always a fun, happy feeling, because that confidence... it has this really sharp edge to it. If I'm in that unstoppable zone, and somebody gets in my way or questions me? I get so incredibly irritated. Like, a small correction from my boss—Brenda, who I mentioned before—if she comes over to my cubicle and just points out that I put a date in the wrong format on a travel voucher, or if a classmate in my evening macroeconomics seminar tries to correct a point I made during a group discussion... I will just snap at them. 

And I mean, I snap at them way, way harder than I mean to. Normally I'm a pretty quiet guy, but when I'm having one of those weeks, I'll practically bite Brenda's head off. I'll start lecturing her about how my way is actually more efficient and she's just bogged down in outdated corporate bureaucracy. Or I'll just completely tear into my classmate over nothing, telling them they aren't looking at the big picture. It's like my skin is buzzing and I'm so high up on this pedestal of my own genius that anyone trying to bring me down to earth or correct my work just feels like an absolute insult. It's embarrassing later, honestly, when the energy wears off, but in the moment, I just can't stop myself from going off on them because I just feel so incredibly right about everything. It just completely takes over.
Before these symptoms started, did you notice a clear decline in your work, school, or social functioning?

Yeah, actually, things were definitely going downhill before the really weird stuff started happening. It was like... well, it was like the foundation was cracking before the house actually started falling apart, you know? 

I mean, I'm taking these evening classes, right? I'm trying to get my degree so I can move up from just being a clerk, and I ended up completely bombing this really important course module. It was for my intermediate financial accounting class, which is usually my bread and butter. I'm usually great at it. But I just couldn't keep the concepts straight. I would sit there staring at the textbook, reading the exact same paragraph about asset depreciation over and over again, and absolutely nothing would stick. So I totally failed that module, which dragged my whole grade down, and it's just super frustrating because I need a certain GPA to even qualify for the CPA track later on. 

And then at work, it was like my brain just stopped processing numbers correctly altogether. I've been doing these same ledgers for over a year. It's completely routine stuff, just matching up the accounts payable and making sure everything balances out perfectly at the end of the week. But suddenly, my ledgers started coming back with these really serious errors. I'm talking transposed numbers, missing decimal points, assigning expenses to completely wrong department codes—stuff I never used to do. Brenda would bring the printouts back to my cubicle and point out all the red ink, and I'd look at them and just have no earthly idea how I messed them up so badly. 

It actually got to the point where I had to start asking for help, which I absolutely hate doing. I had to ask this other clerk, Dave—who sits two cubes down and always chews his gum way too loud—to start double-checking my entries before I submitted them to Brenda, just because I couldn't trust myself anymore. I mean, this is work that used to be so incredibly routine for me. I used to be able to listen to a podcast and knock out twenty expense reports in an hour, no problem. But I just couldn't reliably finish any of it anymore without making these massive mistakes or just losing my train of thought completely. And Dave was definitely getting annoyed having to check my work, and Brenda was clearly losing patience with me, but I just couldn't get my brain to do the simple, routine tasks it used to do on autopilot. And all of that was happening way before I started freezing by the copier or pacing holes in the carpet.
Have you had a marked loss of motivation or drive to start and carry out everyday activities?

Yeah, it's... it's like my battery is just permanently at one percent, you know? It's really frustrating because I want to do things, and I still care about people. I really do. It's not like I've suddenly decided I hate my friends or want to be a hermit or anything like that. But most days... man, most days I just let my phone sit there on my desk. I'll see a text come in, the screen will light up with a message from a buddy, and I'll look at it, and I just absolutely cannot bring myself to reply. The texts just sit unanswered for days because the actual physical and mental effort of typing out a response just feels like climbing a mountain. 

And it's the same with doing things, too. And the very second he spoke and the chair moved, it was like... I don't know, like a switch flipped. I immediately blinked and turned my head and answered him. I told him I was fine and didn't need any food. So I definitely hear people. It is not like I am deaf or totally checked out of reality or locked inside my own head. My ears still work perfectly fine, and my brain processes that someone is talking to me. 

If Brenda at the office says my name, or my roommate asks me a question, or honestly even if a delivery truck honks really loud outside my bedroom window, I snap right back to normal and respond to them. So no, definitely not completely unresponsive. I just need that little external push to get my gears turning again, I guess. And then, of course, I always feel incredibly awkward right after, because I have to act like I wasn't just sitting there like a literal statue. I usually try to play it off, like I pretend I was just deep in thought about an audit report for work or trying to remember a specific tax formula for my evening classes, but I know they probably think it is super weird anyway. doctor.intent: Clarify whether the patient is experiencing disorganized/negatively driven behavior versus catatonic posturing, to help distinguish schizophrenia subtype.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that. I can see why you might ask that, though, like maybe I feel like a puppet on strings or something. But honestly, no. It isn't like some invisible hand is pulling my arms up, or like there's some kind of... I don't know, ghost or magnetic force or mind-control thing happening. It is definitely just me. My own muscles, my own bones. 

When I am standing there by that copier—the big heavy-duty one on the third floor that always smells faintly like burnt plastic when you run more than fifty pages through it at once—it is entirely my own body doing the action. It's just that I don't understand *why* my body is doing it. That's the part that drives me crazy. Like, I know it is my brain sending the signal to lift my hands up, but I just don't know why it's sending that signal in the first place. 

I've actually thought about this a lot. Like, I will be sitting on the bus on my way home from the office—I take the 42 line down past the old shopping center because my car has been making this awful grinding noise in the steering column and I just haven't had the time or the money to take it into a mechanic yet—and I will just be staring out the window, replaying the whole situation with Brenda in my head. And I'll ask myself, 'Did I feel forced? Did someone else make me do that?' And the answer is always no. 

There is no outside pressure, no heavy feeling of someone else guiding my limbs. It is more like... like a glitch in my own programming, if that makes sense. Like my body just decides to hit pause on its own accord and strike this bizarre pose, and my conscious mind is just sort of trapped watching it happen, thinking, 'What in the world are we doing right now?' But it's always me. Just my own confusing, frustrating brain acting up, not any kind of outside force.

doctor.intent: Differentiate disorganized schizophrenia from catatonic schizophrenia by assessing whether the frozen episodes are accompanied by stupor/mutism or other catatonic immobility features rather than just brief odd pauses.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about complete motor immobility or stupor, which is not specifically covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I honestly couldn't tell you if I'm literally unable to move, because... well, because in those moments, the very concept of moving just completely evaporates from my mind. It’s not like I'm fighting against my own body, you know? 

It's not like that sleep paralysis thing. I had a buddy in high school, Jason, who used to get sleep paralysis all the time, and he said it was absolutely terrifying because he would wake up in the middle of the night and try so, so hard to thrash around or yell for his mom, and his body just wouldn't let him do it. He was actively trying to move and couldn't. 

For me, it is nothing like that at all. There is no struggle. When I'm standing by that heavy-duty copier on the third floor, or when I'm staring at the drywall above my peeling particle-board desk, I'm not fighting to put my arms down or turn my head. I'm just... there. The thought of lowering my hands or walking back to my cubicle just doesn't even cross my mind until Brenda says my name or my roommate bumps my chair. 

So I guess I don't really know if I am physically unable to move, because I have never actually tried to break out of it myself while it's happening. It's like my brain just temporarily deletes the instructions for movement, or hits pause on the whole system. My muscles aren't cramped up, I don't feel paralyzed or heavy, but the actual internal command to move just isn't there. So I really can't say for sure if I'm trapped in that position or not, because it never even occurs to me to test the boundaries of it until someone finally snaps me out of it.

Well, I guess I am quiet during it, yeah, but I wouldn't say I'm permanently mute or anything because, like I was saying, the second someone actually speaks to me, I answer them right away. I came in because I have started doing all these things at work and school that just do not make any sense whatsoever, and it's really starting to freak me out.

And then, of course, there's the thing we were just talking about, standing by the copier with my hands held up in the air, just completely silent and frozen, until someone finally walks by and asks if I am okay. Once they ask if I'm alright, I can talk perfectly fine again and I put my hands down. So I'm not mute, I just... I don't say anything while I'm stuck doing these bizarre, pointless things until someone breaks the spell. I just don't get why I'm doing any of it, but it's happening at the office, it's happening during my evening classes, and I just really need to figure out what's wrong with my brain.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the bizarre, disorganized behavior is due to catatonic excitement/markedly disorganized behavior versus a more chronic disorganized/negative-symptom schizophrenia subtype
doctor.question: Have you ever had periods of becoming unusually energetic, agitated, or driven to move around in a way that seems out of control?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: When that energy comes on, I cannot sit through a normal bookkeeping shift without pacing, opening extra tabs, reorganizing files, or feeling like my hands need to keep moving.

patient.answer:
Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It's actually kind of a total 180 from the freezing up thing we were just talking about. It's like... well, it's like a switch flips, and suddenly I have all this buzzing inside my chest and my arms. When that energy comes on, I absolutely cannot sit through a normal bookkeeping shift. I mean, my job is literally just sitting in a chair for eight hours staring at spreadsheets and typing numbers into the system, but when I get like that, sitting still feels physically impossible. It almost hurts to stay seated.

I end up getting up and pacing back and forth in my cubicle—which isn't very big, so it's really just three steps one way, three steps back, over and over again, wearing a path in that same ugly gray carpet I mentioned earlier. And if I try to force myself to sit down and actually do my work, my hands just feel like they need to keep moving. Like they have a motor attached to them. I'll just start opening extra tabs on my computer for no reason. Like, dozens of them. I'll have the company portal open, and then I'll open a tab for a web calculator, and then a blank Google sheet, and then a search for office supplies, just click-click-clicking because my fingers can't stop moving. 

And then I'll look at the physical files on my desk and suddenly decide the entire system is wrong, so I'll start reorganizing files. I'll take all these manila folders—the ones with the little clear plastic tabs that always cut your cuticles if you grab them the wrong way—and I'll pull out all the expense reports and start sorting them by date instead of by vendor name, which isn't even how we're supposed to do it. Brenda actually got really annoyed with me about it last month because she couldn't find the Miller account. But in the moment, I just have so much frantic, nervous energy that I have to be doing *something*, anything, just moving and clicking and sorting at a million miles an hour. It's like I'm driven by this invisible engine and I just can't figure out how to hit the brakes.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the apparent excited/agitated episodes are true manic episodes with mood elevation or not, to distinguish schizophrenia subtype from schizoaffective/bipolar-spectrum illness
doctor.question: During those times when you feel unusually energetic and driven to move, do you also feel abnormally euphoric or overly confident?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of abnormal euphoria or overconfidence during energetic periods, which maps directly to the symptom of elevated or irritable mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah, euphoric is... I mean, confident doesn't even really begin to cover it. It's more like... well, some weeks I just feel unusually sharp, you know? Like my brain is finally operating at a hundred percent capacity and I am just almost completely unstoppable. I'll get home from my evening classes and I won't even be tired. I'll just sit at my particle-board desk in my room and feel like I can map out my entire future in one single night. 

I'll start making these massive, incredibly detailed master plans. Because I'm a clerk, right? So I know how to organize data. I'll start charting out exactly how I'm going to finish my degree early, pass the CPA exam on the first try, start my own auditing firm, and make my first million by the time I'm twenty-five. I'll literally make color-coded spreadsheets for my life goals at three in the morning, and I feel so brilliant while I'm doing it. I feel like I'm the only person on earth who actually understands how the world works, and it's this huge rush. 

But the thing is, it's not always a fun, happy feeling, because that confidence... it has this really sharp edge to it. If I'm in that unstoppable zone, and somebody gets in my way or questions me? I get so incredibly irritated. Like, a small correction from my boss—Brenda, who I mentioned before—if she comes over to my cubicle and just points out that I put a date in the wrong format on a travel voucher, or if a classmate in my evening macroeconomics seminar tries to correct a point I made during a group discussion... I will just snap at them. 

And I mean, I snap at them way, way harder than I mean to. Normally I'm a pretty quiet guy, but when I'm having one of those weeks, I'll practically bite Brenda's head off. I'll start lecturing her about how my way is actually more efficient and she's just bogged down in outdated corporate bureaucracy. Or I'll just completely tear into my classmate over nothing, telling them they aren't looking at the big picture. It's like my skin is buzzing and I'm so high up on this pedestal of my own genius that anyone trying to bring me down to earth or correct my work just feels like an absolute insult. It's embarrassing later, honestly, when the energy wears off, but in the moment, I just can't stop myself from going off on them because I just feel so incredibly right about everything. It just completely takes over.

Yeah, actually, things were definitely going downhill before the really weird stuff started happening. It was like... well, it was like the foundation was cracking before the house actually started falling apart, you know? 

I mean, I'm taking these evening classes, right? I'm trying to get my degree so I can move up from just being a clerk, and I ended up completely bombing this really important course module. I'm talking transposed numbers, missing decimal points, assigning expenses to completely wrong department codes—stuff I never used to do. Brenda would bring the printouts back to my cubicle and point out all the red ink, and I'd look at them and just have no earthly idea how I messed them up so badly. 

It actually got to the point where I had to start asking for help, which I absolutely hate doing. I had to ask this other clerk, Dave—who sits two cubes down and always chews his gum way too loud—to start double-checking my entries before I submitted them to Brenda, just because I couldn't trust myself anymore. I mean, this is work that used to be so incredibly routine for me. I used to be able to listen to a podcast and knock out twenty expense reports in an hour, no problem. But I just couldn't reliably finish any of it anymore without making these massive mistakes or just losing my train of thought completely. And Dave was definitely getting annoyed having to check my work, and Brenda was clearly losing patience with me, but I just couldn't get my brain to do the simple, routine tasks it used to do on autopilot. If I lose count, I have to start the set of nine all over again. doctor.intent: Clarify whether the catatonic-like motor symptoms are more consistent with waxy flexibility/maintenance of imposed posture, which would help distinguish catatonic schizophrenia from other schizophrenia subtypes.

He just kind of leans around the cubicle wall, smacking that loud peppermint gum of his, and goes, "Hey man, you good?" Well, like I was just saying, I don't... I mean, you can try it if you want, but I really don't think it's going to stay there. It's not like my arms are made of wax or clay or whatever.
